title: Shuka goes to King Janaka
word: reading the Isha in the original
hookLine: a son born for the forest is sent to learn freedom from a king
carry: the world and the inner path, held together
tomorrow: what did a sage see when the whole world went under?

lines: A SON BORN FOR THE FOREST.
IF MITHILA BURNS, NOTHING OF MINE BURNS.
cards: Vyasa, the sage tradition credits with the Mahabharata, has a son named Shuka, born, it seems, for the forest: calm, unattached, wanting nothing the world offers.
And Vyasa sends him to learn freedom from, of all people, a king. Janaka of Mithila: a crown, a court, a family, a kingdom to run. Shuka goes.
And he finds that the man who has everything holds none of it tight. The Mahabharata gives Janaka a well-known line: if Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns.

teach.b: That's the picture behind Isha eleven. Vidyam cavidyam ca yas tad vedobhayam saha. Knowing and not-knowing: whoever knows both, together.
Sanskrit says and with a ca after each word, like two hands holding. Then: avidyaya mrityum tirtva, vidyayamritam ashnute. By one, having crossed death; by the other, reaching the deathless.

teach.h: TIRTVA: HAVING CROSSED. TIRTHA: A FORD.
teach.b: Tirtva, having crossed, comes from the same root as tirtha, a ford, the word Hindus use for a holy crossing place on a river. Readers differ on the pair, as yesterday showed.
Many teachers hear it this way: the work of the world and the knowing of the One, held at once, not traded for each other. The Bhagavad Gita names Janaka as its example.
Karmanaiva hi samsiddhim asthita janakadayah: Janaka and others reached perfection through action itself.

teach.h: THE HOUSEHOLDER'S PATH IS A PATH.
teach.b: It's one of Hinduism's steady teachings: the householder's life is a real path. You don't have to leave home to be serious. The monk's way is honored too, and Shuka keeps it.
But the king shows both together can be done: work and family, and an inner life that isn't owned by them.

how: Tirtha, a crossing place, is also the word Hindus use for a pilgrimage place, often on a riverbank; achamana, three sips of water from the right palm, opens many daily pujas.

games.q: what does “reading the isha in the original” mean?
o: reading the Isha as a choice between two kinds of life
reading the Isha's directions to a sacred river
reading the Isha's own words: both kinds of knowing, carried across together

games.q: the king, the monk and the verse — tap the pairs.
p: Vyasa's son, born for the forest
a king who held nothing tight
a ford, a holy crossing place

s: Isha 11 tells you to choose knowing over not-knowing
ubhayam saha: whoever knows both, together.
the Gita names Janaka as someone who reached perfection through action
in Hindu teaching, only monks are on a real spiritual path
the householder's life is a path too; Vyasa sent his monk-born son to learn from a king.

games.q: a cousin says the only serious Hindus are sannyasis; everyone with a job and kids is 'not there yet.' what do the week's verse and story say?
o: the householder's path is real; Janaka is the Gita's own example.
he's right; the Isha says leave the world to cross death.
neither path matters; the Isha says to choose nothing.
games.why: Isha 11 holds both together, and the Gita names Janaka, a working king, as one who reached perfection through action. the monk's way is honored, not required.

practice: If you have water, try achamana, the sip Hindus take before puja: a little water in the right palm, sipped three times, slowly. Many say a name of God with each sip. If you don't pray, just take three slow sips and follow each one.
Then breathe as if wading: in, the near bank, the day's work; out, the far bank, the quiet under it. One crossing, both banks.

wordCard.voice: Reading the Isha in the original, verse eleven: ubhayam saha, both together, and tirtva, having crossed, from the same root as tirtha, a ford.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: tirtva, having crossed, from the root of tirtha, a ford.

carryVoice: Your line: the world and the inner path, held together. Janaka did it with a crown on. See you on the far bank.
